title: Yom Kippur: ask first
hook: before the day, people ask one another's forgiveness

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shabbat Shuvah and Hosea's call. Your line was return. Today, the one thing Yom Kippur can't do by itself.

The afternoon before Yom Kippur has its own sounds. Phones buzzing with messages: if I hurt you this year, I'm sorry. Neighbors stopping each other on the street. A teenager, mortified, knocking on a sister's bedroom door. Some of it is a little formal, a habit. Some of it is the hardest conversation of the year. People do this because of one line in the Mishnah, and once you hear it, the whole holiday looks different.
screen: `PHONES BUZZING: I'M SORRY.` → `A KNOCK ON A SISTER'S DOOR.` → `ONE LINE IN THE MISHNAH.`

segments.voice: The line is at the very end of tractate Yoma, the Mishnah's book about Yom Kippur. Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah teaches: for wrongs between a person and God, Yom Kippur atones. For wrongs between a person and another person, Yom Kippur does not atone, until you have appeased the other person. A whole day of fasting and prayer, the day the Torah sets aside for atonement, cannot fix what you did to your neighbor. Only your neighbor can. So you go first. You ask. The Talmud and later law work out the details. Later authorities say to name what you did, not stay vague. If the person refuses, you try again, up to three times, bringing a few friends along to help make peace. If they still refuse after that, the burden lifts from you. There's a rule for the other side, too. Maimonides writes that a person shouldn't be cruel and refuse to forgive: when someone sincerely asks, forgive with a whole heart and a willing spirit. Not every hurt can be fixed in an afternoon. Teachers are careful to say that forgiveness isn't the same as trust, and that no one is required to put themselves back in danger. But the shape is clear. Before you stand before God asking to be forgiven, stand in front of the people you hurt. Then the day can do its work. The Hebrew word for this kind of forgiveness is mechilah, which some teachers explain as letting go of a debt.
screen: `BETWEEN YOU AND GOD.` · `BETWEEN YOU AND YOUR NEIGHBOR.` · `UP TO THREE TIMES.` · `DON'T BE CRUEL; FORGIVE.` · then, large: `ASK BEFORE THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Go past the obvious one and look for the hurt you filed as too small or too old to mention, a joke at someone's expense, a promise that quietly lapsed, a message never answered, and name the specific thing, the way the later authorities ask. Then turn it around, as Maimonides does: is someone trying to ask you, and have you made it hard for them? If you pray, you can ask God for an open hand in both directions.
Yom Kippur. The day of atonement, which, the Mishnah says, can't atone for wrongs between people until they make peace.
Your line: ask before the day. Between people, it's the people who have to come first. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In the days before Yom Kippur, especially on its eve, many Jews ask family, friends and coworkers for forgiveness (mechilah), and many say a prayer before Kol Nidre declaring that they forgive anyone who wronged them.

chat.says: If I fast and pray on Yom Kippur, does that cover how I treated my brother?
options: The Mishnah says the day atones between you and God; with people, you ask them first.
The Mishnah says the fast covers everything, as long as you pray hard enough.

chat.meaning: Mishnah Yoma 8:9: Yom Kippur atones for wrongs between a person and God, but not between people until you appease the one you hurt.

notes: Mishnah Yoma 8:9 teaching attributed to Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah; confirm.

Maimonides Hilchot Teshuvah 2:10: do not be cruel; forgive with a whole heart; confirm.
Forgiveness vs. trust and safety: a widely taught modern clarification, not from these sources; a Keeper may want a citation.
